title: Quickly, not badly
hookLine: don't say someone bathes badly, say quickly, until you know his reasons (Enchiridion 45)

lines: EVERYONE ELSE LINGERS AT THE BATHS.
ONE MAN IS OUT IN TEN MINUTES.
cards: A man walks into the public baths, washes, and is out the door in ten minutes, while everyone else lingers over the hot water, the oil and the gossip. Everyone notices.
And everyone has the same word ready: he bathes badly. Sloppy. Rude.
Doesn't know how it's done. Section forty-five of the handbook takes that one word and swaps it for another. It's a tiny edit, and it changes what you're claiming to know.

teach.b: Someone bathes quickly, Epictetus says. Don't say he bathes badly; say he bathes quickly. Someone drinks a lot of wine.
Don't say he drinks badly; say he drinks a lot. Why? Until you know the judgment behind what he's doing, how do you know it's bad?
Maybe the quick bather has a sick child at home. Maybe he's late for work, or the water is cold, or he simply doesn't like crowds. You saw the speed.
You didn't see the reason. Keep to this, Epictetus says, and you won't end up grasping some impressions clearly and then agreeing to others you never actually saw. Quickly is something you saw.
Badly is something you added. The habit spares you a thousand small, confident mistakes about other people.

A twentieth-century psychologist, Marshall Rosenberg, built a whole approach to hard conversations, which he called Nonviolent Communication, on a similar first step: separate what you observe from how you evaluate it.
You came home at midnight is an observation.

You're irresponsible is a judgment. Two very different teachers, a long way apart, each with their own reasons, both noticing that people can hear a description without bracing for a fight. A judgment usually starts one.

how: Some people practicing Stoicism describe other people's actions in plain, observable terms before making any judgment about them, as Epictetus suggests in Enchiridion 45.

o: doing a hard task fast to get it over with
acting at once, before a doubt can creep in
describing what you saw instead of adding a verdict

games.q: quickly, not badly — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says to praise everyone's habits
he says describe them. you don't know the reason, so don't call it bad.
Epictetus' second example is someone who drinks a lot of wine
don't say he drinks badly. say he drinks a lot.

games.q: your roommate leaves dishes in the sink overnight. what fits Enchiridion 45?
o: the dishes were in the sink overnight.
games.why: describe what you saw. until you know the reason behind it, you don't know it's bad.

practice: Think of someone whose habits bother you: the coworker who's always late, the neighbor who mows at seven, the relative on the phone at dinner.

Notice the word you usually reach for, rude, lazy, thoughtless, then try Epictetus' swap and say only the description inside: late, early, often on the phone. Notice what happens to the irritation when the judgment drops out.

wordCard.voice: Quickly. Epictetus' swap: say he bathes quickly, not badly, because you saw the speed, but not the reason. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: quickly, the word Epictetus puts in place of 'badly' in Enchiridion 45.

carryVoice: Your line: say what you saw. Quickly is seen; badly is added. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication (observation versus evaluation)
